chunks: Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan, from Bakr ibn Salih, from Ali ibn Asbat, from al-Hasan ibn al-Jahm, from Bukayr ibn A'yan who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Are the Knowledge of God and His Will different or the same?
So he said: Knowledge is not the Will. Do you not see that you say 'I shall do such-and-such if God wills it' and you do not say 'I shall do such-and-such if God knows it'?
So your saying 'if God wills it' is evidence that He has not yet willed it. So when He wills, that which He wills comes to pass, just as He wills it — and the Knowledge of God precedes the Will.

key_terms.إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ: If God wills — the Islamic conditional formula used for future intentions, itself a theological proof of the distinction between Knowledge and Will
key_terms.عِلْمُ اللَّهِ: The Knowledge of God — eternal, prior, unchanging; encompasses all things before and after creation
key_terms.مَشِيئَة: Mashiyyah — Divine Will/Volition; in Shia theology this is an attribute of divine action, not essence; it is what actualizes divine decree

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between God's Knowledge and God's Will in Shia theology?
ai.summary: In this hadith, Bukayr ibn A'yan — a trusted companion of Imams al-Baqir and al-Sadiq — poses a profound theological question to Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him): are God's Knowledge and His Will distinct attributes or identical? The Imam responds with a linguistic-philosophical argument: the common Islamic formula 'insha'Allah' (if God wills) presupposes that God has not yet willed an outcome, even while He has eternally known it. This demonstrates that mashiyyah (Will/Volition) is a distinct attribute of divine action — it is contingent and actualizing — while 'ilm (Knowledge) is prior and necessary. The hadith belongs to the chapter on Will as an attribute of divine act, reflecting the Shia theological distinction between God's eternal essential attributes and His volitional/active attributes.
